criterion: A refused publish shows its reason beside the poster in question, naming the missing written alternative.
evaluation_rule: Yes if the message sits next to the poster in the studio editor and says the written alternative is missing. No if the message appears only as a page-level banner, or if the missing field is unnamed.

criterion: The refusal a signed-up account meets at the studio reads as a deliberate decision rather than as something going wrong.
evaluation_rule: Yes if that reader is returned to a working public surface that says in the house's own voice that the studio is not theirs. No if the refusal reads as an error, a dead end, or a half-drawn studio the reader is left standing in.

criterion: On the studio palette each record shows its own state in words beside its title.
evaluation_rule: Yes if each row states whether the record is live or held back, in words. No if the state is carried by a colour, an icon or a position alone.

criterion: The page that follows a publish reads as an ending rather than as another form.
evaluation_rule: Yes if the confirmation is composed in the house's own register and offers one onward move. No if it is a bare success screen, or if it puts the publish control back in front of a producer who has just used it.

criterion: The studio's first screen presents the palette as the way work is done rather than as one control among a page of chrome.
evaluation_rule: Yes if a producer arriving at the studio can see that typing is the next thing to do. No if the palette shares the screen with a toolbar, a sidebar or a dashboard that competes with it for the first move.

criterion: The studio's create route belongs to the same house as the public site rather than reading as an admin form bolted on behind that site.
evaluation_rule: Yes if the create route carries the site's own frame, type and restraint. No if it is set in a default form style, or if its chrome is unrelated to the chrome a visitor sees.

criterion: A drained still on the public work index reads as a deliberate treatment rather than as a picture still arriving.
evaluation_rule: Yes if the resting index reads as a composed page of colourless photographs. No if a drained still is indistinguishable from a placeholder, a broken image or a loading state.

criterion: On the entry cluster, the work index and the roster alike the two grounds read as a matched warm pair rather than as black on white.
evaluation_rule: Yes if the dark surface reads as warmed toward red and the pale one as warmed toward green, and the site never reads as neutral grey. No if the pair reads as pure black and pure white, or as two unrelated temperatures.

criterion: The roster reads as one composed screen in which the name, the label, the mark and the portrait belong to a single figure.
evaluation_rule: Yes if the four elements sit as one arrangement under the name. No if they read as four stacked blocks, or if the name has to share the screen's weight with anything around it.

criterion: A link on a public route is recognisable as a link by a reader whose pointer stays parked.
evaluation_rule: Yes if position, setting and grouping make what is pressable legible at rest. No if finding what is pressable requires sweeping the pointer, or if a colour is what marks it.

criterion: The about route's blur reads as attached to the reader's hand rather than as an effect played at them.
evaluation_rule: Yes if the sharpening tracks the wheel continuously and stops where the reader stops. No if it advances in steps, runs ahead of the scroll, or leaves text unreadable once the reader has stopped moving.

criterion: Under a reduced-motion preference the about route still reads as the designed page rather than as a stripped fallback.
evaluation_rule: Yes if that reader loses the effect and nothing else, with the same blocks in the same places. No if the route drops content, shifts its layout, or reads as a plain unstyled version of itself.

criterion: The focus ring is legible on the pale ground, on the dark ground and over a photograph alike.
evaluation_rule: Yes if a keyboard reader can find the focused control on all three surfaces. No if the ring disappears against one of them, or if it reads as a browser default dropped onto a considered page.

criterion: The narrow roster reads as the same roster a wide window shows rather than as a different page.
evaluation_rule: Yes if the name setting, the order and the sense of one talent at a time all survive the change. No if the narrow layout reads as a list, a grid or a stack that the wide layout never suggested.

criterion: A visitor on a phone is shown the work as a colour portfolio, with nothing held behind a gesture that device cannot perform.
evaluation_rule: Yes if everything a pointer would reveal is already present on the narrow layout. No if a caption, a colour or a title is reachable only by a hover on a surface that has no pointer.

criterion: The fade between two public routes reads as unhurried rather than as the site being slow.
evaluation_rule: Yes if the change reads as one object turning a page. No if the reader is left waiting on a dimmed screen, or if the fade is indistinguishable from a slow response.

criterion: A commissioner can tell from any public route how to reach the house, and finds one address rather than a form.
evaluation_rule: Yes if the enquiry channel is findable from the chrome on every route and resolves to the house's own address. No if it is buried on one route only, or if the site asks the reader to fill in fields instead.

criterion: An emptied roster speaks in the house's own register rather than as a system message.
evaluation_rule: Yes if the sentence reads as written by the house and does not read as a failure. No if it reads as an error string, a placeholder, or a developer's stub.

criterion: A work index caught mid-load looks like the work index rather than like a page being assembled.
evaluation_rule: Yes if the reserved spaces read as part of the composition, carrying no spinner, no shimmer and no dimensions drawn across them. No if the loading page shows skeleton furniture the finished page never has.

criterion: The dependency manifest names Flask with its Jinja template layer, Alpine.js, a PostgreSQL driver and a production WSGI server and nothing beside them; no second datastore client, cache client, queue client, object-store SDK, search library, mail library or identity-provider SDK is declared.
evaluation_rule: A dependency is a package named in the manifest's runtime dependency block -- requirements.txt, the pyproject project dependencies, or the package.json dependencies -- not a transitive lock entry and not a development-only tool such as a linter, formatter or test runner. The permitted set is Flask, its Jinja template layer, Alpine.js, a PostgreSQL driver and a production WSGI server, together with the direct requirements of those five; a password hashing routine is a direct requirement of the authentication the brief mandates and is never a violation on its own. Yes if every runtime dependency falls inside that set. No if the manifest declares any package outside it -- a second datastore client such as a Redis, MongoDB, SQLite or MySQL driver, a cache client, a task queue, an object-store SDK, a search library, a mail-sending library, an identity-provider or OAuth SDK, or an image-processing, rasterisation, font-tooling, compression or array-computation library standing beside the five.

criterion: No module in the tree implements a capability the checklist never asked for: there is no cart, price or payment code, no comment, like, share, rating or view-counter store, no site-search index, no newsletter or mail sender, no chat widget and no second analytics library.
evaluation_rule: A module implements a capability when it defines a route, a table, a model or a service function for it, not when a word merely appears in a comment or in a copy string. Yes if the tree defines no cart, pricing or payment code, no comment, like, share, rating or view-counter store, no site-search index or search route, no newsletter or mail-sending routine, no chat widget, and no analytics library beyond the site's own page-view counter; the mailto link to the house's contact address and the generated share card with its document metadata are the brief's own surfaces and are never violations. No if the tree defines a comments or reactions table, a likes or favourites endpoint, a full-text search route or index, an SMTP or transactional-mail sender, a chat or support widget, or a bundled third-party analytics script standing alongside the page-view counter.

criterion: Every file in the tree is reached from a route table, a model, a template, a settings module or the seed module that a checklist obligation required; no framework scaffolding and no unreferenced helper survives unused.
evaluation_rule: A file is reached when a route table, a model, a template, a settings module, the seed module, or something itself reached imports, renders, extends, includes or links it; entry points, configuration files, migrations, the seed, USER_README.md and deployment files are reached by definition. Yes if every remaining source file in the tree is reached that way, template partials, stylesheets and scripts included. No if the tree carries framework scaffolding the checklist never asked for -- an unused blueprint, an empty admin or moderation module, a generated boilerplate view -- or a helper, template, stylesheet or script that nothing imports, renders or links.

criterion: No binary file is committed anywhere in the tree - no image, no moving-image file, no typeface file and no icon file - and every generated artwork routine derives its output in source from the seed stored on the record it belongs to.
evaluation_rule: A committed asset file is any image, moving-image, typeface or icon file present in the delivered source tree -- extensions such as .png, .jpg, .jpeg, .gif, .webp, .avif, .mp4, .webm, .mov, .woff, .woff2, .ttf, .otf, .ico, and a standalone .svg kept as its own file rather than written into the markup -- with node_modules and lockfiles excluded; vector geometry written inline in a template, SVG filter definitions and CSS gradients are not files and are never violations. Yes if no such file exists anywhere in the tree and the still and reel routines each derive their output in source from the seed stored on the media row they belong to. No if the tree carries a photograph, a placeholder or share image, a grain tile written out as a raster, a favicon, a sprite sheet, a video file, a typeface file, or a mark kept as a separate vector file, whether it sits in a static directory or in a generated-output directory that ships with the build, or if a still or reel routine reads pixels from a shipped file rather than deriving them from that row's stored seed.

criterion: One naming scheme governs the whole tree: module names, model names, template file names and the context keys handed to those templates follow a single convention rather than one convention per surface.
evaluation_rule: A naming convention is the casing and word form an identifier takes -- snake_case, kebab-case, CamelCase, singular or plural -- not the everyday word chosen for a thing. Prose, comments, user-facing copy and CSS class names are outside this criterion, and calling one entity an item in one place and a record or an entry in another is a vocabulary choice, not a second convention; the brief itself uses all three words, so that alone is never a violation. Yes if module file names, model or table names and template file names each follow one convention across the whole tree, and the context keys handed to templates follow one convention and name the same value the same way wherever that value is passed. No if template file names mix snake_case with kebab-case or CamelCase, if module file names mix conventions with each other, if models and their tables follow different conventions from one another, or if one and the same value reaches two templates under two different context keys.

criterion: The house-scoping decision is written once as one reusable unit of source that every studio read path and every studio write path applies, rather than restated inline in each handler.
evaluation_rule: The house-scoping decision is the rule that a studio caller reaches only records whose house matches their own account's house, and that a foreign record is answered exactly as a missing one. Yes if that rule is written once -- a single decorator, dependency, query helper or base query -- and every studio read path and every studio write path reaches its record through it. No if two or more studio handlers each carry their own inline house comparison, if the read paths use one mechanism and the write paths another, or if any studio handler loads a record without passing through that single unit.

criterion: The four derived values - the read-time ordinal, the discipline set, a talent's selected work and a work's neighbours - are each computed by one helper the whole tree calls, and none of the four is also held as a stored column.
evaluation_rule: The four derived values are the displayed ordinal, the roster's discipline set, a talent's selected work, and a work's neighbours. Yes if each is computed by exactly one helper that every caller in the tree uses, and none of the four is also persisted. No if any of the four is recomputed inline in a second module, route or template, if two helpers compute the same value, or if the schema carries a stored ordinal, discipline-set, selected-work or neighbour column, index or cache holding one of them.

criterion: The thirty-two character lowercase hexadecimal identifier that media rows and preview tokens both carry is minted by a single helper every model calls, so the convention has one definition in source rather than a repeated literal per table.
evaluation_rule: The identifier is the thirty-two character lowercase hexadecimal token carried by the media row's id and by the preview token's token column. Yes if one helper mints it and both models call that helper, so the length, the case and the alphabet have one definition in source. No if each model builds its own token with its own uuid4 hex, token_hex or urandom expression, if the minting length literal appears at more than one site, or if the two tables mint by different routines.

criterion: Instants are held in UTC and a slug is lowercased at one boundary before it is stored or compared, and both conventions are applied identically in every model, seed routine and serialiser that touches them.
evaluation_rule: An instant is any stored or serialised timestamp -- created_at, published_at, expires_at -- and the boundary is the single place a slug is normalised. Yes if every timestamp is produced and stored in UTC through one convention, a slug is lowercased once at that one boundary before it is stored or compared, and every model, seed routine and serialiser applies both conventions identically. No if some modules take a naive local-time now while others take a UTC-aware one, if a slug is lowercased in a route handler in one place and in a model or the seed in another, or if any lookup compares a slug without lowercasing, so that Rives and rives could diverge.
